questions.question: What is @RestController in Spring Boot?
questions.title: @RestController annotation explained
questions.direct_answer: @RestController is a Spring annotation that combines @Controller and @ResponseBody. It marks a class as a web controller and automatically serializes method return values to JSON (or XML) in the HTTP response body. This eliminates the need to annotate every method with @ResponseBody, making REST API code cleaner and more concise.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the composition of @RestController and its role in building REST APIs.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying it's just for making controllers without mentioning that it automatically handles response body serialization.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that @RestController uses Jackson by default for JSON serialization and explain why this matters for REST APIs versus traditional MVC views.

sections.title: What @RestController Does and Why It Exists
sections.content: **@RestController** is a specialized Spring stereotype annotation introduced in Spring 4.0 specifically for building RESTful web services. Before @RestController existed, developers had to use **@Controller** to mark a class as a Spring MVC controller and then add **@ResponseBody** to every single method to tell Spring to serialize the return value directly into the HTTP response body instead of rendering a JSP or Thymeleaf template. Think of @RestController as a convenience shortcut: it's literally **@Controller + @ResponseBody combined into one annotation**. When you annotate a class with @RestController, Spring automatically applies @ResponseBody behavior to all methods in that class. The framework uses **Jackson** (the default JSON library) to convert your Java objects into JSON and write them to the response. This is essential for REST APIs where clients expect structured data (JSON or XML) rather than HTML pages. The annotation signals intent clearly: this controller handles data endpoints, not views.

sections.title: Building a Simple User REST Controller
Key Points
content: **@RestController**: Combines @Controller and @ResponseBody into a single annotation for REST endpoints.
**Automatic JSON serialization**: Spring Boot uses Jackson to convert return values to JSON without additional configuration.
**No view resolution**: Unlike @Controller, @RestController methods never trigger view template rendering — the return value IS the response.
**Method-level overrides**: You can still use @ResponseBody on individual methods in a @Controller class if only some methods return data.
**Content negotiation**: By default returns JSON, but can return XML if the client sends Accept: application/xml and you have the right dependencies.
**Component scanning**: @RestController is a stereotype annotation, so Spring Boot auto-detects it during component scanning.
**Exception handling**: Combine with @ControllerAdvice to handle exceptions globally and return structured error responses.

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: At RestController is a Spring annotation that combines at Controller and at ResponseBody. It's specifically designed for building REST APIs. When you put at RestController on a class, Spring treats every method's return value as the actual HTTP response body, not as a view name. So if a method returns a User object, Spring automatically converts it to JSON using Jackson and sends that JSON back to the client. Before at RestController existed, you had to use at Controller on the class and then put at ResponseBody on every single method. That was repetitive and error-prone. The at RestController annotation saves you that hassle. For example, if you're building an endpoint that returns user data, you just write a method that returns a User or List of User, and Spring handles all the JSON conversion for you. One thing freshers often miss: at RestController is only for data endpoints. If you're building a traditional web app with HTML pages, you'd still use at Controller and return view names. But for modern REST APIs, at RestController is the standard choice because it makes the code cleaner and communicates intent clearly.

speakable_v2.hook: @RestController is just two annotations merged into one — and knowing which two tells you exactly what it does.

beats.text: @RestController combines @Controller and @ResponseBody into one class-level annotation. @Controller tells Spring MVC this class handles HTTP requests. @ResponseBody tells Spring to serialize the return value directly to the HTTP response as JSON — don't look for a view template.

Before @RestController existed, you had to add @ResponseBody to every single method in a REST controller. @RestController applies it at the class level so you write it once. In a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application, Jackson is already on the classpath via starter-web, so it handles the Java-to-JSON conversion automatically. You just return objects.

questions.question: What is the difference between @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping?
questions.title: HTTP method mapping annotations in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: @GetMapping maps HTTP GET requests to a method and is used for read operations. @PostMapping maps POST requests for creating resources. @PutMapping maps PUT requests for full updates or replacements. @DeleteMapping maps DELETE requests for deletions. All four are shorthand for @RequestMapping with a specific method attribute, making REST controller code more readable and intentional.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands HTTP verb semantics and knows the standard Spring annotations for mapping them.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @PostMapping for everything or not knowing that these annotations map to specific HTTP methods.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the REST convention that GET is idempotent and safe, POST is not idempotent, PUT is idempotent, and how this affects API design.

sections.title: HTTP Method Mapping Annotations Explained
sections.content: Spring Boot provides four specialized annotations for mapping HTTP methods to controller methods: **@GetMapping**, **@PostMapping**, **@PutMapping**, and **@DeleteMapping**. These are convenience annotations introduced in Spring 4.3 as shortcuts for the more verbose **@RequestMapping** with a method parameter. Before these existed, you'd write @RequestMapping(value = "/users", method = RequestMethod.GET), which was repetitive. Now you just write @GetMapping("/users"). Each annotation corresponds to a specific HTTP verb and REST operation: GET for reading data, POST for creating new resources, PUT for full updates, and DELETE for removing resources. Using the correct annotation improves code readability because the HTTP method is immediately visible. It also enforces REST conventions: GET and DELETE typically don't have request bodies, while POST and PUT do. Spring's dispatcher servlet uses these annotations to route incoming HTTP requests to the correct method based on both the URL path and the HTTP verb.

sections.title: CRUD Operations with HTTP Method Annotations
Key Points
content: **@GetMapping**: Maps HTTP GET requests, used for safe read-only operations that don't modify server state.
**@PostMapping**: Maps HTTP POST requests, used for creating new resources (not idempotent — calling twice creates two resources).
**@PutMapping**: Maps HTTP PUT requests, used for full updates or replacements (idempotent — calling twice produces the same result).
**@DeleteMapping**: Maps HTTP DELETE requests, used for removing resources (idempotent — deleting twice is the same as deleting once).
**Shorthand annotations**: All four are aliases for @RequestMapping with method = RequestMethod.GET/POST/PUT/DELETE.
**Path composition**: These annotations inherit the base path from class-level @RequestMapping if present.
**Request body**: @PostMapping and @PutMapping typically use @RequestBody to deserialize JSON; @GetMapping and @DeleteMapping usually don't.

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: These four annotations map different HTTP methods to controller methods. At GetMapping is for reading data, so you'd use it for endpoints that fetch user profiles or product lists. It maps to HTTP GET requests, which are read-only and don't change anything on the server. At PostMapping is for creating new resources. When a client wants to create a new user or order, they send a POST request with the data in the body. It's not idempotent, meaning if you call it twice you get two resources. At PutMapping is for updating or replacing an existing resource. You'd use it for endpoints that update a user's profile or change a product's details. It's idempotent, so calling it multiple times with the same data produces the same result. At DeleteMapping is for deleting resources. It's also idempotent because deleting something twice is the same as deleting it once. All four are just shortcuts for at RequestMapping with a method parameter. Using the specific annotations makes your code clearer because anyone reading it immediately knows what HTTP method the endpoint accepts. A common mistake freshers make is using at PostMapping for everything. In REST APIs, you should match the HTTP verb to the operation: GET for reads, POST for creates, PUT for updates, DELETE for deletes.

speakable_v2.hook: Each HTTP verb has its own mapping annotation — and each maps to a specific CRUD operation in REST design.

beats.text: All four are shortcuts for @RequestMapping with a specific HTTP method pre-set. They exist purely for readability. Here's the standard REST mapping used in a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application.

rows: Read — fetch a resource or list
Replace — update an existing resource fully

beats.text: Always use the specific annotation — @GetMapping is far clearer than @RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.GET). They communicate intent in one glance.

questions.question: What is the difference between @PathVariable and @RequestParam?
questions.title: @PathVariable vs @RequestParam in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: @PathVariable extracts values from the URL path itself, like /users/123 where 123 is the user ID. @RequestParam extracts values from query strings, like /users?status=active where status is a parameter. Path variables identify which resource you're working with, while request parameters filter, sort, or modify how you retrieve that resource.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands URL structure and the semantic difference between path segments and query parameters.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @RequestParam for resource identifiers or not knowing that @RequestParam reads from the query string.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that path variables are part of the resource identity (RESTful), while query params are optional modifiers, and explain required vs optional parameter handling.

sections.title: Understanding Path Variables vs Query Parameters
sections.content: **@PathVariable** and **@RequestParam** both extract data from the incoming HTTP request, but from different parts of the URL. @PathVariable pulls values from the URL path segments themselves — the parts between slashes. For example, in /api/users/42, the 42 is part of the path and identifies a specific user resource. @RequestParam pulls values from the **query string** — the part after the question mark. In /api/users?status=active&page=2, both status and page are query parameters. The key difference is semantic: path variables are about **resource identity** (which user, which order), while query parameters are about **filtering, sorting, pagination, or optional modifiers**. REST design conventions say you should use path variables for required identifiers and query params for optional criteria. Spring makes both easy: annotate a method parameter with @PathVariable or @RequestParam, and the framework extracts and converts the value automatically.

rows: Yes, but use required=false to make optional
Searching users by status or pagination

sections.title: When to Use Each Annotation
sections.content: **Use @PathVariable** when the value identifies a specific resource or is logically part of the resource hierarchy. For example, /api/orders/101/items/5 uses two path variables: orderId (101) and itemId (5). This clearly shows you're fetching item 5 within order 101. Path variables should be required and meaningful — they define what resource you're operating on. **Use @RequestParam** when the value is an optional filter, sort criterion, pagination parameter, or any modifier that doesn't change which resource you're addressing. For example, /api/products?category=electronics&minPrice=100&page=2 uses query params because you're still fetching products, just with filters applied. Query params are often optional (use required=false in the annotation). A good rule of thumb: if removing the parameter makes the URL point to a different resource or makes no sense, it should be a path variable. If removing it just returns unfiltered or default results, it should be a query param.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **@PathVariable**: Extracts values from URL path segments like /users/{id}, used for resource identifiers.
**@RequestParam**: Extracts values from query strings like ?status=active, used for filters and modifiers.
**REST semantics**: Path variables are part of resource identity; query params are optional constraints or pagination.
**Required by default**: Both are required by default in modern Spring; use required=false to make @RequestParam optional.
**Type conversion**: Spring automatically converts path/query string values to method parameter types (Long, Integer, Boolean, etc.).
**Multiple path variables**: You can have multiple path variables like /orders/{orderId}/items/{itemId} for nested resources.
**Default values**: Use defaultValue in @RequestParam to provide a fallback if the parameter is missing.

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: At PathVariable and at RequestParam both pull data from the URL, but from different places. At PathVariable extracts values from the path itself. So if your URL is slash users slash 123, you'd use at PathVariable Long id to get that 123. It's for identifying which specific resource you're working with. At RequestParam extracts values from the query string, the part after the question mark. So if your URL is slash users question mark status equals active, you'd use at RequestParam String status to get that active value. Query parameters are usually optional filters or search criteria. The key difference is intent. Path variables say which resource you want. Query params say how you want to filter or modify the request. In REST design, you'd use path variables for required identifiers and query params for optional stuff like pagination or sorting. For example, GET slash orders slash 42 uses a path variable for the order ID. But GET slash orders question mark status equals shipped and page equals 2 uses query params to filter and paginate. Spring makes both easy to use. You just annotate the method parameter and Spring extracts and converts the value for you. One thing to watch out for: both are required by default, so if a query param is optional, you need to add required equals false.

speakable_v2.hook: Both extract values from the URL — but from different parts. Path variable is which resource, query param is how to filter it.

beats.text: The difference is where in the URL the value comes from.

Mental model that works: path variable answers 'which resource?' — GET /users/42 fetches user 42. Query parameter answers 'how should the response be shaped?' — GET /users?status=active&page=1 filters and paginates the list. In a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application, you'll use both in the same controller all the time.

questions.question: What is @RequestBody and how does it work?
questions.title: @RequestBody in Spring Boot REST controllers
questions.direct_answer: @RequestBody is a Spring annotation that tells the framework to read the HTTP request body and deserialize it into a Java object. It's used with POST, PUT, and PATCH methods that receive JSON or XML data. Spring Boot uses Jackson by default to convert the incoming JSON into your Java class by matching field names.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands how request payload deserialization works in Spring REST APIs.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that @RequestBody triggers automatic JSON-to-object conversion or thinking you need manual parsing.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Jackson as the default deserializer, explain how field name matching works, and note that you can use validation annotations with @RequestBody.

sections.title: How @RequestBody Deserializes HTTP Payloads
sections.content: **@RequestBody** is the annotation that enables Spring to read the HTTP request body and automatically convert it into a Java object. When a client sends a POST or PUT request with JSON data in the body, Spring needs to know which method parameter should receive that data. That's where @RequestBody comes in. You annotate a method parameter with @RequestBody, and Spring's **HttpMessageConverter** (specifically **MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter** for JSON) reads the raw request bytes, parses the JSON, and creates an instance of your Java class with the fields populated. The conversion is bidirectional: just as @ResponseBody converts Java objects to JSON responses, @RequestBody converts JSON requests to Java objects. Spring Boot configures Jackson as the default JSON processor, so you don't need any XML configuration. Jackson uses reflection to match JSON field names to Java field names or getter/setter method names. If the JSON has a field called "username", Jackson looks for a Java field named username or a method named setUsername(). This automatic deserialization is what makes building REST APIs so fast — you write business logic with plain Java objects, and Spring handles all the HTTP and JSON plumbing.

sections.title: Creating a Resource with @RequestBody
Key Points
content: **@RequestBody**: Tells Spring to deserialize the HTTP request body into a Java object using Jackson.
**Automatic conversion**: Spring Boot auto-configures Jackson to convert JSON to Java objects and vice versa.
**Field name matching**: Jackson maps JSON field names to Java field names or setter methods automatically.
**POST/PUT/PATCH**: @RequestBody is used with methods that receive data in the request body, not with GET or DELETE.
**Validation support**: Combine with @Valid to trigger Bean Validation and reject invalid payloads before they reach your code.
**Content-Type header**: The client should send Content-Type: application/json so Spring knows how to deserialize the body.
**Single parameter**: You typically use @RequestBody on one parameter per method (the payload object), not multiple parameters.

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: At RequestBody tells Spring to read the HTTP request body and convert it into a Java object. It's used with POST, PUT, and PATCH methods where the client sends data in the body, usually as JSON. When you annotate a method parameter with at RequestBody, Spring uses Jackson to parse that JSON and create an instance of your Java class. For example, if a client sends a POST request to create a user with JSON like username colon john and email colon john at example dot com, Spring automatically converts that into a User object with those fields populated. You don't have to manually parse the JSON or read input streams. Jackson matches the JSON field names to your Java field names. If the JSON has a username field, Jackson looks for a username field in your User class or a setUsername method. One common mistake freshers make is forgetting that the client needs to send Content-Type application slash json header so Spring knows it's JSON. Another thing: you can combine at RequestBody with at Valid to trigger validation. If the incoming data fails validation, Spring returns a 400 Bad Request automatically. So at RequestBody is basically the input side of REST APIs. You use it to receive data from clients, and Spring handles all the deserialization for you.

speakable_v2.hook: @RequestBody is the bridge between the JSON in the request body and your Java object — Jackson handles the conversion.

beats.text: When a client POSTs a JSON body, Spring needs to turn that JSON string into a Java object. @RequestBody triggers that. Jackson reads the JSON field names and maps them to matching Java fields on your DTO. If the client sends name and email, Jackson creates a CreateUserRequest with those fields populated — no manual parsing needed.

The power move is combining @RequestBody with @Valid. @RequestBody handles format parsing — if the JSON is malformed, it fails with a 400. @Valid then validates the constraints declared on the DTO fields (@NotBlank, @Email). In a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application, using both annotations on a @PostMapping parameter gives you format safety and business rule validation in one line.

questions.question: How do you return different HTTP status codes in Spring Boot?
questions.title: HTTP status codes in Spring Boot — ResponseEntity and @ResponseStatus
questions.direct_answer: You can return custom HTTP status codes in two main ways: use @ResponseStatus on a method or exception class to set a fixed status code, or return ResponseEntity<T> from your method to dynamically control the status, headers, and body. ResponseEntity is more flexible because the status can change based on logic, while @ResponseStatus is simpler for fixed responses.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows how to properly signal HTTP status codes beyond the default 200 OK.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Always returning 200 OK for everything, or not knowing that ResponseEntity gives full control over the HTTP response.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain when to use each approach, mention common status codes (201 Created, 204 No Content, 404 Not Found), and note that ResponseEntity can include custom headers.

sections.title: Two Ways to Control HTTP Status Codes
sections.content: Spring Boot provides two primary mechanisms for setting HTTP status codes in REST controllers. The first is **@ResponseStatus**, which is an annotation you put on a method or exception class to declare a fixed status code that Spring should return. For example, @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED) on a POST method tells Spring to return 201 instead of the default 200. The second approach is **ResponseEntity<T>**, which is a class you use as your method's return type. ResponseEntity wraps your response body and lets you set the status code, headers, and body all in one object. The key difference: @ResponseStatus is compile-time and fixed, while ResponseEntity is runtime and dynamic. If your status code depends on business logic — like returning 404 if a resource isn't found or 201 if it was created — you need ResponseEntity. If every invocation of a method should return the same status, @ResponseStatus is simpler and more declarative.

rows: Less code, cleaner for fixed status

sections.title: When to Use Each Approach
sections.content: **Use @ResponseStatus** when the status code is the same for every successful execution of the method. For example, a POST endpoint that always creates a resource should return 201 Created, so you can annotate the method with @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED) and just return the created object. This is clean and declarative. Also use @ResponseStatus on custom exception classes: if you have ResourceNotFoundException, annotate it with @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND), and whenever that exception is thrown, Spring automatically returns 404. **Use ResponseEntity** when the status code depends on the result. For example, a PATCH endpoint might return 200 OK if the resource was updated or 404 Not Found if it doesn't exist. ResponseEntity lets you write conditional logic: return ResponseEntity.ok(resource) or return ResponseEntity.notFound().build(). ResponseEntity also gives you full control over response headers, which @ResponseStatus does not. If you need to return a Location header after creating a resource or set Cache-Control, you must use ResponseEntity.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **@ResponseStatus**: Annotation that sets a fixed HTTP status code for a method or exception class.
**ResponseEntity**: A return type that wraps the response body and provides dynamic control over status, headers, and body.
**Common status codes**: 200 OK (default GET/PUT), 201 Created (POST), 204 No Content (DELETE), 404 Not Found, 400 Bad Request.
**ResponseEntity builders**: Use .ok(), .created(), .noContent(), .notFound() for readable status construction.
**Exception mapping**: Annotate custom exception classes with @ResponseStatus to auto-map exceptions to HTTP codes.
**Headers**: Only ResponseEntity can set custom headers using .header(name, value).
**Default behavior**: Without @ResponseStatus or ResponseEntity, Spring returns 200 OK for successful methods.

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: There are two main ways to return different HTTP status codes in Spring Boot. The first is using the at ResponseStatus annotation. You put it on your method, and it tells Spring what status code to return. For example, if you have a POST endpoint that creates a user, you'd put at ResponseStatus HttpStatus dot CREATED on the method, and Spring returns 201 instead of the default 200. This works great when the status is always the same. The second way is using ResponseEntity as your return type. ResponseEntity lets you control the status code, headers, and body all in one object. So you can write logic like if the user exists return ResponseEntity dot ok with the user, otherwise return ResponseEntity dot notFound dot build. That gives you 200 or 404 depending on the result. ResponseEntity is more flexible but also more verbose. A common pattern is using ResponseEntity dot ok or ResponseEntity dot status and then dot body to set both the code and the data. You can also set headers with dot header if you need that. One thing freshers miss: proper status codes matter. Don't just return 200 for everything. Use 201 for creates, 204 for successful deletes with no body, 404 for not found, 400 for bad input. REST APIs communicate through status codes, so using the right one makes your API easier to use.

speakable_v2.hook: Spring defaults to 200 OK. To return 201, 204, or a dynamic 404, you need to take control of the status code.

beats.text: Two ways to control the HTTP status code in a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application. For a fixed status that's always the same, add @ResponseStatus on the method — @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED) makes a POST return 201 every time, @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT) makes a DELETE return 204.

For dynamic status codes that depend on the result, use ResponseEntity as the return type. ResponseEntity.ok(user) returns 200 with the user body. ResponseEntity.notFound().build() returns 404 with no body. You can chain these with Optional.map() to return 200 if the record exists and 404 if it doesn't — in a single line. ResponseEntity also lets you set custom response headers when needed.

questions.question: What is @ControllerAdvice and how do you handle exceptions globally in Spring Boot?
questions.title: @ControllerAdvice for global exception handling
questions.direct_answer: @ControllerAdvice is a Spring annotation that lets you handle exceptions globally across all controllers in one centralized class. You combine it with @ExceptionHandler methods to catch specific exceptions and return custom error responses. This eliminates the need to write try-catch blocks in every controller method and ensures consistent error handling throughout your REST API.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows how to implement centralized exception handling instead of repeating error logic in every controller.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using try-catch in every controller method or not knowing that @ControllerAdvice provides global exception interception.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @ControllerAdvice uses AOP behind the scenes, mention returning structured error responses with custom fields, and note that you can restrict it to specific packages or controllers.

sections.title: Global Exception Handling with @ControllerAdvice
sections.content: **@ControllerAdvice** is a Spring annotation that marks a class as a global exception handler for all controllers in your application. Without it, every controller method would need individual try-catch blocks to handle exceptions like ResourceNotFoundException or ValidationException. That leads to duplicated error-handling code scattered across your app. @ControllerAdvice solves this by centralizing exception handling in one place. You create a class annotated with @ControllerAdvice, and inside it you define methods annotated with **@ExceptionHandler** that specify which exception types they handle. When any controller throws an exception, Spring's **DispatcherServlet** checks if a @ControllerAdvice class can handle it. If a matching @ExceptionHandler is found, Spring invokes that method instead of propagating the exception. The handler method can return a ResponseEntity with a custom error body and HTTP status code. This approach keeps your controllers clean (they just throw exceptions) and ensures consistent error responses across your entire API. Behind the scenes, @ControllerAdvice uses **aspect-oriented programming (AOP)** to intercept exceptions.

sections.title: Centralized Exception Handler with Custom Error Response
Key Points
content: **@ControllerAdvice**: Marks a class as a global exception handler that applies to all controllers in the application.
**@ExceptionHandler**: Annotates methods inside @ControllerAdvice to specify which exception types they handle.
**Centralized error handling**: Eliminates the need for try-catch blocks in controllers and ensures consistent error responses.
**Custom error responses**: You can return structured error objects with fields like error code, message, timestamp, and validation details.
**HTTP status mapping**: Use ResponseEntity to return appropriate status codes (404, 400, 500) for different exception types.
**AOP behind the scenes**: @ControllerAdvice uses aspect-oriented programming to intercept exceptions before they reach the client.
**Scoped advice**: You can restrict @ControllerAdvice to specific packages or controller classes using annotations like @ControllerAdvice(basePackages).

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: At ControllerAdvice is a Spring annotation that lets you handle exceptions globally across all your controllers. Without it, you'd need try-catch blocks in every controller method, which leads to a lot of duplicated code. With at ControllerAdvice, you create one class that handles all exceptions in a centralized way. Inside that class, you write methods annotated with at ExceptionHandler. Each method specifies which exception it handles. For example, you'd have one method for ResourceNotFoundException that returns a 404, and another for IllegalArgumentException that returns a 400. When any controller throws an exception, Spring checks your at ControllerAdvice class to see if there's a matching handler. If it finds one, it calls that method instead of crashing. The handler method returns a ResponseEntity with a custom error response and the right HTTP status code. This keeps your controllers clean because they just throw exceptions and don't worry about formatting error messages. It also ensures all your error responses have the same structure. A good practice is to create a custom ErrorResponse object with fields like error code, message, and timestamp. Then every error response looks consistent. One thing to mention: at ControllerAdvice uses aspect-oriented programming behind the scenes to intercept exceptions. It's a powerful feature that makes your API more maintainable.

speakable_v2.hook: Without @ControllerAdvice, every controller method needs its own try-catch. With it, you handle all exceptions in one place.

beats.text: @ControllerAdvice is a class-level annotation that makes a class an interceptor for exceptions thrown by any controller in the application. You add @ExceptionHandler methods inside it — each one handles a specific exception type. When UserController throws a ResourceNotFoundException, your advice class catches it, runs your handler method, and returns the structured error response you define.

In a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application, use @RestControllerAdvice instead — it combines @ControllerAdvice and @ResponseBody so your error response objects serialize to JSON automatically. One class handles all your exception-to-HTTP-response mappings: ResourceNotFoundException becomes 404, MethodArgumentNotValidException becomes 400, any unhandled RuntimeException becomes 500. Consistent error format across the entire API.

questions.question: What is @RequestMapping at the class level used for?
questions.title: @RequestMapping class-level base path
questions.direct_answer: @RequestMapping at the class level sets a base URL path prefix for all methods in that controller class. If a class has @RequestMapping("/api/users") and a method has @GetMapping("/{id}"), the full URL is /api/users/{id}. This avoids repeating the base path on every method and logically groups related endpoints under one path prefix.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands URL path composition from class-level and method-level mappings.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that class-level paths combine with method-level paths, or thinking the class annotation overrides method annotations.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that this keeps controller code DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself), mention that you can also set common headers or consumes/produces at the class level.

sections.title: URL Path Composition with Class-Level @RequestMapping
sections.content: **@RequestMapping** at the class level defines a **base URL path** that applies to all handler methods in that controller. This is one of Spring MVC's key organizational features. Instead of writing the full path on every method (like @GetMapping("/api/users/{id}"), @PostMapping("/api/users"), @DeleteMapping("/api/users/{id}")), you declare the common prefix once at the class level: @RequestMapping("/api/users"). Then each method only specifies its unique path segment. Spring combines the class-level path and method-level path to form the full URL. For example, if the class has @RequestMapping("/api/orders") and a method has @GetMapping("/{orderId}/items"), the final URL is /api/orders/{orderId}/items. This follows the **DRY principle** (Don't Repeat Yourself) and makes refactoring easier: if you need to change the base path from /api/orders to /v2/orders, you only change it in one place. The class-level @RequestMapping can also set common attributes like headers, consumes (accepted Content-Type), or produces (response Content-Type), which then apply to all methods unless overridden.

sections.title: Class-Level Path Composition Example
Key Points
content: **Base path prefix**: Class-level @RequestMapping sets a common URL prefix for all methods in the controller.
**Path composition**: Spring concatenates class-level and method-level paths to form the full URL.
**DRY principle**: Avoids repeating the base path on every method, making code cleaner and easier to refactor.
**Logical grouping**: Groups related endpoints under one path, making the API structure clear (e.g., all user operations under /api/users).
**Shared attributes**: Class-level @RequestMapping can set common headers, consumes, or produces that apply to all methods.
**Method override**: Method-level annotations can override class-level settings if needed.
**Empty path**: A method with @GetMapping with no path inherits only the class-level path.

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: At RequestMapping at the class level sets a base URL path that applies to all methods in that controller. So if you put at RequestMapping slash api slash products on your controller class, every method's path gets that prefix. If a method has at GetMapping slash curly brace id, the full URL becomes slash api slash products slash id. Spring automatically combines the class path and the method path. This is really useful because you don't have to repeat the base path on every single method. It keeps your code DRY, which stands for Don't Repeat Yourself. If you need to change the base path later, like from slash api slash products to slash v2 slash products, you only change it in one place instead of updating every method. It also makes the controller structure clearer. Anyone reading the code can immediately see that this controller handles all product-related endpoints because they're all grouped under the same base path. You can also use class-level at RequestMapping to set common attributes like headers or the Content-Type that all methods should use. Method-level annotations can override those if needed. One thing to note: if a method has just at GetMapping with no path, it maps to exactly the class-level path. So at GetMapping at the method level maps to slash api slash products if that's your class path.

speakable_v2.hook: Class-level @RequestMapping sets a base path so you don't repeat /users on every single method.

beats.text: @RequestMapping on the class sets a root path that all method-level mappings are relative to. Add @RequestMapping('/users') to the class, then @GetMapping('/{id}') on a method, and the full URL becomes GET /users/{id}. Without the class-level mapping, you'd have to write /users/{id} on every method annotation — repetitive and error-prone.

The standard pattern in a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application: one controller class per resource, with the resource base path on the class. UserController has @RequestMapping('/api/v1/users'). OrderController has @RequestMapping('/api/v1/orders'). Methods then only declare the relative path — /{id}, /search, whatever they handle. URL versioning also happens here — bump the class-level path to /api/v2/users when you need to version an endpoint.
